```{r}

x + y
x * 2

z + short
z + c(1, 0, 1)

fruits <- append(fruits, "date")
append(fruits, "kiwi", after = 1)
```

## Part 4 — Lists: Creating and Subsetting
```{r}
student <- list(
  name = "Maria Santos",
  age = 20,
  grades = c(88, 92, 79),
  is_enrolled = TRUE
)
class(student["grades"])
class(student[["grades"]])
student$name
student$grades[2]
```
10. The single bracket just prints out the just the list because the grades is in the list and the double bracket is the contents of the grades 
11. The short answer is that a vector is homogeneous and a list is not, which changes what “give me element 2” can mean.

##Part E — Critical Thinking Challenge
```{r}
inventory <- list(
  item = c("Notebook", "Pen", "Eraser"),
  price = c(25.50, 10.00, 5.00),
  in_stock = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)
inventory$item[inventory$in_stock]
inventory$item <- append(inventory$item, "Ruler")
inventory$price <- append(inventory$price, 15.00)
inventory$in_stock <- append(inventory$in_stock, TRUE)
inventory$item
inventory$price
inventory$in_stock

```
12. First, R evaluates inventory$in_stock using the $ operator to extract its underlying logical vector of TRUE and FALSE values. Next, R aligns this logical vector element-by-element with the corresponding positions of inventory$item. Finally, the single brackets [ ] use those boolean values as a positional filter, retaining only the item names that share an index with a TRUE value while dropping any that correspond to FALSE.
13. keeping data in separate vectors risks silent data corruption—such as items becoming permanently mismatched with their prices if one vector is modified or sorted without updating the others—whereas grouping them into a list or data frame guarantees that all attributes remain bound to the correct item.

Conclusion
Vectors are homogeneous data structures that store elements of a single data type, making them ideal for mathematical operations, sequences, and filtering tasks where consistency is required. In contrast, lists are heterogeneous containers capable of holding elements of varying types and structures, such as mixed vectors or even other lists, which makes them essential for grouping related datasets together. You would choose a vector for uniform numerical or categorical computations, whereas a list (or its extension, the data frame) is the preferred choice when encapsulating complex, multi-attribute records to ensure data integrity and structural alignment.
